title: The Enhanced ACT: Complete Overview
summary: How the enhanced ACT is built: sections, timing, the composite score, the English and Reading formats, and a 6-week study plan.

blocks.text: This page explains the whole enhanced ACT in one place: the sections, the timing, how the composite score is made, what an ACT English passage and an ACT Reading passage look like, and how to plan your preparation. Read it once carefully before you start the lessons, then come back to it the week before your test.
What the enhanced ACT is

The ACT is a college admission test that many American Diploma students take. Since **September 2025** every ACT is the **enhanced ACT**: the same design is used for all tests, **online and paper**, in the United States and internationally. If you find an old book or video that describes a longer test with more questions, it is describing the old ACT. Use the numbers on this page.

The ACT is **not adaptive**. Everyone taking the same test form gets the same questions, and the questions do not get easier or harder because of your answers. (This is a big difference from the Digital SAT, where your Module 1 result decides the level of Module 2.) On the ACT a hard question is simply a hard question, and every question in a section is worth the same.
The sections at a glance
The three **core** sections (English, Math and Reading) take **125 minutes** of testing time in total. This course covers the two verbal core sections, **English** and **Reading**.

blocks.title: Unscored questions
blocks.text: Each core section contains some questions that do not count towards your score (10 in English, 4 in Math, 9 in Reading). You cannot rely on knowing which ones they are, so treat every single question as if it counts.

rows: Fast. Most grammar questions should take 20–30 seconds, which saves time for the 'whole passage' questions.
This includes the time to read long passages, so you cannot read slowly and re-read everything.

blocks.text: How the composite score works

Your **composite score** is on a scale of **1–36**. It is the **average of your English, Math and Reading scores**. Science and Writing are reported separately: they appear on your score report but they do not raise or lower the composite.

items: Because the composite is an average, a strong English score can balance a weaker Math score, and the other way round.
English is usually the section where students improve fastest, because the grammar and punctuation rules are limited and they repeat on every test.
We do not give target scores or university requirements on this site. Requirements differ from university to university and change from year to year, so check each university's own admissions page.

blocks.text: The optional sections: Science and Writing

**Science** (40 questions, 40 minutes) and **Writing** (one essay, 40 minutes) are optional. You choose whether to take them when you register. Neither one changes your composite. Whether you need them depends only on the universities you apply to, so find out early from each university's admissions page and decide before you register.

ACT English: what the section looks like
ACT English is not a list of separate sentences. You read **essays** and fix them while you read. The **scored** part of the section is built like this:

The essays are of three kinds: **informational** (explains a topic, a person, a discovery), **argumentative** (gives an opinion and supports it) and **narrative** (tells a story, often in the first person). You do not need any background knowledge; everything you need is in the passage.
Underlined portions and NO CHANGE

Most questions refer to an **underlined portion** of the passage, marked with a question number. The question shows four versions of that portion. The first choice is very often **NO CHANGE**, which means "keep the original". Many questions have **no written question at all**: you simply see the four versions and choose the best one. Here is the shape (original example; the underlined portion is shown in bold):
**Passage:** "The first lighthouse on this coast was built of wood, **it burned down** [12] within ten years."
**Choices:** A) NO CHANGE   B) wood, and it burned down   C) wood it burned down   D) wood, burning it down

**Answer: B.** The original joins two complete sentences with only a comma (a comma splice). B adds "and", which makes the join correct. C has no punctuation at all (a run-on). D changes the meaning: it now says the wood burned the lighthouse down. Notice that NO CHANGE is a real choice: on some questions the original is already the best version, and then A is the answer.
Questions about the passage as a whole
Some questions have no underlined portion. They ask about a sentence, a paragraph or the whole essay. The stem then tells you exactly what to decide, for example:

items: whether the writer should **add** a new sentence at a certain point, or **delete** a sentence, and why;
where a sentence or a paragraph should be **placed** so that the essay is logical;
which choice gives the most effective **introduction, conclusion or transition**;
whether the essay **achieves a goal** the writer had in mind ("Suppose the writer's goal had been to…").

blocks.text: For these questions you must understand what the paragraph and the essay are about, which is why you should read the passage as you answer, not jump from underline to underline.
The three reporting categories of ACT English
Every scored English question belongs to one of three categories. The percentages are shares of the scored questions; the last column shows where each skill is taught in this course.

headers: What it means in practice (course pages)
rows: Relevance (add/delete), transitions, order of sentences and paragraphs, purpose and goal questions — Relevance; Organization and Order
Precise word choice, concision (cutting extra words), consistent style and tone — Concision; Word Choice and Tone
Punctuation, grammar and usage, sentence structure — Punctuation; Grammar and Usage; Sentence Structure

ACT Reading: what the section looks like
The Reading section has **36 questions in 40 minutes**. The **scored** part is built from **three passages with 9 questions each**:

In total there is **one literary narrative** (a story or a memoir) and **two informational passages** from the humanities, social science or natural science. On each form, one of the sets is special: it is either a **pair of passages** on the same topic (with questions that compare them) or a passage that comes with **charts or graphs** (with questions that connect the text and the data).

rows: Main idea, details, inferences, summaries, cause and effect, sequence
Meaning of words in context, the author's purpose and point of view, how a paragraph or sentence functions
Comparing paired passages, using charts or graphs, judging claims and evidence

blocks.text: The Reading part of this course gives you a method for 650–750-word passages and a full lesson on each of the three categories.
Rules that change how you take the test

items: **No penalty for wrong answers.** A blank and a wrong answer both score zero, so **answer every question**. Never leave a bubble or a screen empty.
**Not adaptive.** Every question in a section is worth the same, so do not get stuck on a hard one. Answer, mark it if you can, and move on.
**Online or paper.** The enhanced design is the same in both. Practise with a clock either way.
**The official information** is on act.org. If anything there is different from this page, follow act.org.

blocks.text: A 6-week study plan for ACT English and Reading

Plan for about **45–60 minutes a day, 5 days a week**. If you have more time, repeat the weeks where your quiz scores were lowest. Keep a **mistake notebook**: for every wrong answer write the rule or the trap in one line.

rows: This overview; How to Attack ACT English; ACT Punctuation
Know the format. Learn every comma, semicolon, colon, dash and apostrophe rule.
ACT Grammar and Usage; ACT Sentence Structure
Agreement, pronouns, verb forms, idioms; fragments, run-ons, modifiers, parallel structure.
Concision; Relevance (add/delete); Organization and Order; Word Choice and Tone
The 'rhetorical' questions: what to cut, keep, move and choose.
Reading strategy; Key Ideas and Details
A method for long passages; main idea, detail and inference questions.
Craft and Structure; Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
Vocabulary in context, purpose, paired passages, charts and graphs.
Full timed practice. Review every explanation, including for questions you got right.

blocks.title: How to study each lesson page
items: Read the rules and the ✓/✗ examples slowly and copy the key rule into your notebook.
Cover the answer of each worked example and try it yourself first.
Take the quiz at the end without looking back at the lesson.
Read the explanation of **every** question, not only the ones you got wrong. A correct guess is still a gap in your knowledge.

blocks.title: Classic mistakes about the ACT
items: Leaving questions blank. There is no penalty, so a blank is always a lost chance.
Reading a whole English essay first and answering afterwards. Answer as you read.
Thinking that NO CHANGE is a trick and never choosing it — or choosing it whenever you are unsure. Judge it like any other choice.
Spending two minutes on one English question. At about 42 seconds per question, one long fight costs you three easy points later.
Studying from old materials that describe the longer pre-2025 test.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: English: read until the end of the sentence that contains the underline, then look at the choices.
Look down the four choices and ask: what is changing? That tells you which rule is being tested.
When two choices are both grammatically correct and say the same thing, the shorter one is usually right.
Reading: share the 40 minutes evenly between the passages and check the clock after each one; never spend extra minutes on one question.
Answer every question before time is called.

blocks.text: Check your understanding

This short untimed test has two parts. Questions 1–4 check that you understand how the test works. Questions 5–8 are real-format ACT English items on one short narrative essay; the numbers in the passage show which underlined portion each question refers to.

blocks.title: Enhanced ACT format check + 4 sample English items
blocks.intro: 8 questions, untimed. Questions 1–4 check that you know how the test works. Questions 5–8 are sample ACT English items on one short essay.

questions.q: How many questions does the ACT English section have, and how much time do you get?
c: 50 questions in 35 minutes
75 questions in 45 minutes
54 questions in 64 minutes
40 questions in 40 minutes
questions.e: English has 50 questions (40 of them scored) in 35 minutes, which is about 42 seconds per question. 54 questions in 64 minutes describes the Digital SAT Reading and Writing section, and 40 in 40 is the optional Science section.

questions.q: Which section scores are averaged to give the ACT composite score (1–36)?
c: English, Math and Reading only
All five sections, including Science and Writing
English, Math, Reading and Science
English and Reading only
questions.e: The composite is the average of English, Math and Reading. Science and Writing are optional and are reported separately, so they do not change the composite.

questions.q: Thirty seconds remain in the English section and you have four questions you have not answered. What is the best thing to do?
c: Leave them blank, because a wrong answer loses points
Choose an answer for every one of them, because there is no penalty for wrong answers
Answer only the first one carefully and leave the rest
Choose NO CHANGE for all four, because it is always the safest answer
questions.e: The ACT has no penalty for wrong answers, so a guess can only help you. NO CHANGE is not a 'safe' answer; it is correct only when the original is truly the best version.

questions.q: Which description matches the scored passages of the ACT English section?
c: Single sentences, each with one blank to fill
Two long passages with twenty questions each
Many short passages of 25–150 words with one question each
Five essays (informational, argumentative or narrative) with questions about underlined portions and about the passage as a whole
questions.e: ACT English uses five scored essays: three of about 340 words with 10 questions each and two of about 185 words with 5 questions each. One short passage per question is the Digital SAT format.

questions.q: [5] Choose the best version of the underlined portion.
c: NO CHANGE
The oven which my grandfather built decades ago, still
The oven, which my grandfather built decades ago; still
The oven, which my grandfather built decades ago, still
questions.e: "which my grandfather built decades ago" is extra information, so it needs a pair of commas: one before and one after. A opens the pair but never closes it; B closes it but never opens it; C uses a semicolon, which cannot end an extra-information phrase.
questions.p:
Every morning before sunrise, my grandmother lit the clay oven behind her house in Fayoum. __The oven, which my grandfather built decades ago still__ [5] stands beside the old lemon tree, its sides blackened by thousands of fires. The thick walls of the oven __holds__ [6] the heat for hours, so one fire can bake bread for half the street.

My grandmother never used a recipe. She never measured the flour or timed the dough. __For example,__ [7] her loaves came out the same every time: puffed, golden and slightly smoky. When I asked her how she knew the bread was ready, she laughed and said that her hands could hear it.

Fayoum is also known for its large lake, which attracts many birds in winter. [8] Last summer I finally tried to bake on my own. My first loaves were flat and burned at the edges, but my grandmother ate one anyway and told me to come back the next day. I did, and I have gone back every morning since.

questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion.
c: NO CHANGE
holding
hold
has held
questions.e: The subject is "walls" (plural), not "oven", which is inside the phrase "of the oven". Plural subject → plural verb "hold". A and D are singular forms; B is not a complete verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

questions.q: [7] Choose the best version of the underlined portion.
c: NO CHANGE
Even so,
Similarly,
In other words,
questions.e: She measured nothing, yet her loaves were always the same: that is a surprise, so the transition must show contrast. "Even so" does this. A treats the result as an example of not measuring; C signals a similar idea; D signals a restatement.

questions.q: [8] The writer is considering deleting the sentence just before number 8 ("Fayoum is also known… in winter."). Should the writer delete it?
c: No, because it describes the setting the reader needs in order to picture the grandmother's house
No, because it explains why the grandmother started baking bread
Yes, because it moves the focus away from the grandmother, the oven and the narrator's baking
Yes, because it contradicts the earlier statement that the oven stands beside a lemon tree
questions.e: The essay is about the grandmother's oven and the narrator learning to bake. The lake and the birds are off-topic, so the sentence should go. A and B give reasons the sentence does not support; D invents a contradiction that is not there.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Core sections: English 50 q / 35 min, Math 45 q / 50 min, Reading 36 q / 40 min — 125 minutes in total.
Composite (1–36) = average of English, Math and Reading. Science and Writing are optional and separate.
English: 5 scored essays (3 × about 340 words with 10 questions, 2 × about 185 words with 5 questions); underlined portions; NO CHANGE is a real option.
Reading: 3 scored passages × 9 questions; one literary narrative and two informational; one paired set or one passage with graphs.
Not adaptive and no penalty: answer every question.
